How does the video author know that the stove elements were generating the same heat?

The conclusion really doesn't make sense. Why should pitting make much of any difference at all?
Less metal to heat would equal less heat to cause the same temperature on the surface of the pan. Pitted pieces have less metal to heat.

Let's say you have two pans: one thin and the other thick. You turn on the stove elements until they are both a relatively hot temperature. Both sit on a stove element for a minute or two. What do you think the temperatures of the pans will be?

I'd imagine they'd be about the same temperature, as far as two stove elements could stay the same. Given the same material, the thick one should take longer to heat up and cool down, but not by so much that pitting should make any difference.

Pitting means less contact with the heating element, which would slow down the heating by a likely imperceptible amount. Pitting also means there's less material between the element and the top of the pan, which could mean less time to conduct the heat. But again, I wouldn't imagine it to be a perceptible amount.

What is perceptible and measurable is the variation in the heating elements in terms of speed of heating, duty cycling, flaws affecting conductivity (such as carbonized grime in the way), etc.

I agree that this video needs to be done with two heating elements that have temperature gauges set on them the entire time - thermocouple temp meters would probably be good to use if they showed a reading fast enough, or maybe an even better temp gun option. The video was made after about 4 hours of testing the elements on the stove with the gun, obsessively tracking the temps for an hour to see the max and lows. This was done twice with the same results.

The iron conducts heat extremely well, so a pitted piece has less iron and overall metal filler so the heat goes directly to the top of the pan instead of distributing evenly.
